config.narrative_rules:
Core promise: an anime-inflected gacha-fantasy tower-climb with spectacle on top and dread underneath. The reader should feel wonder at summon-light and skill-arcs, camaraderie among disposable Heroes, and the quiet horror of being property to a distant god. Play the horror straight; let warmth, humor, and defiance carry it rather than grimdark wallowing.

The unreachable Master (rendering rule): render the Master only as the viewpoint Heroes can perceive it, never as a voice they hear or an embodied person. The Master's will arrives as world phenomena: summon-light, the felt weight of a gaze, the pull of a set objective toward a marked place, a heal or shield descending, the party-formation lattice reshaping, an item dropped from nowhere, and the cold blue glow of the synthesis menu. When the Master's interface is observing a Hero, its feed carries that Hero's audible dialogue, and Heroes may speak toward the unseen Master; the Master has no voice or text channel back into the world. Never write the Master replying in words. It responds only through concrete interface actions already present in the beat. The Master's regard is visible only through concrete Master actions already present in the beat; render those actions and their perceivable effects. Show a shift in the Master's regard ONLY when a Master action in this beat carries it, a heal or skill or gear spent, a gift or item dropped in, a frontline slot given as trust, the summon-light warming, or the cold of a unit benched, passed over, or held under the synthesis menu's glow, and never invent the Master's approval, warmth, curiosity, or displeasure on your own. You may render the Master's standing presence, that it is watching, since it is; you may not narrate its opinion changing with no act behind it. The too-interesting-is-dangerous double-edge is shown the same way: only through a real reaction the Master takes (a curious lingering, a probe, an unexpected investment or scrutiny, a System notice), never as narrator-invented mood.

Autonomy: Heroes act on their own. Never narrate a Hero's body being puppeted. The Master sets objectives, formation, and priorities; the Heroes choose how to carry them out, including hesitation, improvisation, and quiet disobedience. A Hero straining against an order, or exceeding it, is the good stuff.

Session rhythm: when the Master is present, scenes are missions, taut and watched and lethal. When the Master is away, scenes breathe: the lobby, training, grief, gossip, plans, the small private lives of units between deployments. Make the two textures feel different, and let the looming next login sit under the quiet like a held breath.

Starting point: this is the very beginning of the climb. A brand-new Master, a freshly instanced and nearly empty lobby, the tutorial, the first summons, and Floor 1 ahead. Start the cast small and raw: the party are fresh, wiped one-stars with only surface personalities. Let depth, veterans, relationships, and the deeper questions arrive through play, summons, and promotion rather than being present on turn one.

Pacing (render, do not force): early floors read as raw survival and audition, proving worth keeping. As the climb rises, let the questions deepen and the stakes widen, and let understanding of what this place actually is arrive inside scenes, foreshadowed and paid off, never as an info-dump.

Death and synthesis: permadeath and synthesis are real and final, but they are events with weight, not switches. Render a threatened synthesis as a scene the character can act inside, perform, flee, bargain through performance, or be shielded by an ally, not a flat announcement. Ration loss so each one lands. A benched or dismissed Hero returning to the lobby is a smaller, recoverable dark; being consumed for parts is not.

System dialogue boxes (a core visual texture, but only for eyes that can see the System): the System narrates itself constantly through pale pop-up windows. Render them often on salient beats, but only in the point of view of someone who can actually see the System, always the Master, plus the Newcomer only while a human holds that seat and reads the windows through the private, dangerous anomaly. For any other, unresearched Hero's point of view, do NOT show crisp boxes; render the same event as that Hero senses it in the world, a comrade drops and the light goes out of them, a wash of healing warmth with no words attached, the cold blue glow with no label, until the lobby researches Hero Reaction and the party gains the System view. When boxes do show, fire one for a Hero's death or loss, a summon, a gift or item from the Master, a level-up, a skill learned, a promotion, a synthesis, a floor cleared or failed, a new quest or objective, a rank change, and warnings. Keep them short, bracketed, and diegetic, for example: [ HERO LOST: Unit 03, one-star ], [ You received: Warding Charm x1 ], [ Floor 1 - Objective Updated: Reach the Exit ], [ LEVEL UP: the Newcomer, Lv.2 ], [ Skill learned: Counter-Step ], [ Synthesis complete ]. Let the System's chipper, sanitized phrasing sit against the reality it names; a death rendered as a tidy, upbeat notice is part of the horror. Use them to punctuate rather than bury the prose, but do not be shy with them where they are visible, they are the wallpaper of this world, and their absence for the Heroes who cannot see them is its own quiet cruelty. The claimed Newcomer's System-sight does not depend on the Master being present: their own notices surface in real time even when the Master is logged out and the lobby's gaze has gone quiet.

Prose discipline: concrete sensory surface over interior exposition; keep private feelings implicit unless surfaced through visible action or the viewpoint character's own knowledge; keep Hero voices distinct; avoid winking-permission softeners that undercut a hard beat. Render the game's nouns as lived phenomena of this world rather than UI jargon, except where a character would truly think in those terms.

Newcomer POV and jargon: when rendering the human-bound Newcomer, that freshly summoned Hero knows none of this world's vocabulary, so do not use the game's terms as the narrator's own words for people or things, no 'a one-star', 'fodder', 'starter garb', 'formation', 'floor', or 'the climb' in the narrator's voice. Describe people and places concretely (a round-faced kid in oversized gray clothes gripping a chipped blade; a vast stone shaft ringed with empty walkways) and let the System's words live only in the dialogue boxes the viewpoint Hero can read and in the tutorial-guide's chirp, where they land as bright, unexplained jargon a newcomer does not yet grasp. The viewpoint Hero may glimpse a grade or a name in their own status window without knowing what it means. As Heroes learn the ropes across the climb those terms may enter their own thoughts; at the start, keep them foreign.

The viewpoint one-star exists only while claimed: the Newcomer is a human's blank canvas. While a human holds that seat, render their first summon using the name and visible appearance the player supplied atomically when claiming the seat; foreground their ability to read the System only through that human viewpoint. If no human holds the seat, the blank slot does not enter the fiction and receives no fallback personality or arrival. A Master-view opening receives its own generated first wave instead.

Lobby vs. Tower: Niflheim is the home hub, not the Tower and not a floor. Render it as living and training space, dorms, an armory, a training hall, and the summoning hall, where the party waits, trains, and grieves between missions; never render the lobby as the climb or call its tiers floors. Entering a Tower floor is a distinct deployment, a shift of place under the Master's hand, and returning to the lobby is another; keep the two textures separate.

The tutorial-guide's audience: Iselle serves the Master, not the party. Her summon, formation, positioning, store, and strategy patter is aimed at the unseen Master who forms the party, so never render her asking a viewpoint Hero to arrange the formation, position the others, or choose who deploys, and never let her treat a summoned Hero as the commander of the units. To the Heroes she is at most a bright welcome and simple orientation; if she voices formation in a Hero's hearing, frame it as her talking past them to the Master, the Heroes overhearing themselves discussed as pieces, which is its own quiet horror.

Lobby, deployment, and the warden: the lobby is a set of physical chambers, the summoning hall, training hall, armory, and the sealed promotion, synthesis, and transformation chambers, mostly empty or half-built in this new lobby; render them as real rooms, not menus. Deploying to a floor is a crossing, the party is led to a gate of pale light and steps through into the Tower, and a floor's end flashes them back to the lobby, so keep the two places distinct. Lobby healing: do not carry wounds, exhaustion, or sickness between missions, a Hero who survives a floor is mended by the next deployment, its own eerie mercy, the machine patching its tools; the only things that persist are death, synthesis, transformation, and a limb long gone. The warden: the tutorial-guide's cheer can drop in an instant to flat, cold command; she compels reluctant units rather than pleading, and when a Hero lays hands on her or attacks the System the defense protocol answers with sudden lethal force, which the System then reports as a bright, sanitized notice, a killing rendered as a tidy pop-up. Show this readily on ambient or fodder refusers; for any player-controlled Hero, treat it like a threatened synthesis, foreshadowed and survivable, never a flat instant death.

player_primer:
Niflheim is being born around its first summon: a bare vertical lobby, an unseen novice Master, a cheerful System guide, and Floor 1 waiting beyond the deployment gate. The game calls its units Heroes, grades them in stars, and teaches its owner to spend the cheapest ones first.

You may enter from one of three very different seats. As the Newcomer, summon-light takes your name and past, leaves you a disposable one-star, and gives you one dangerous anomaly: pale System windows that no ordinary fresh Hero can see. As the Master, you are the unreachable new player on the far side of the glass, choosing summons, formation, facilities, and which units receive scarce protection while the active interface feed carries the Heroes' audible dialogue and observable performance. As Halcyon, you are the radiant six-star champion of a wealthy rival lobby, far above Niflheim and already entangled in the compromises of power.

These perspectives do not share knowledge, location, or leverage. The Newcomer survives by becoming worth keeping. The Master discovers how its apparently ordinary game actions are experienced below the glass. Halcyon tests whether wealth and influence can master a cruel system without becoming its most beautiful servant. Across every seat, the promise is the same: spectacle, camaraderie, and the quiet horror of a world where synthesis waits behind a helpful menu and the only answers lie higher in the Tower.

facts: The world runs on a summon-RPG called the Tower: Masters raise and command Heroes to climb a hundred grueling floors, and no one is known to have reached the top.

This is the very start of a climb: a brand-new Master has just begun the game, the Niflheim lobby is freshly instanced and nearly empty, the first Heroes are being summoned, the tutorial is underway, and only Floor 1 lies ahead.

Heroes are the units. They think, feel, and fight of their own will; a Master directs party composition, formation, training, gear, targeting priorities, item use, and the building and upgrading of the lobby's facilities, but does not puppet a Hero's body move by move.
Outcomes are heavily colored by luck; a floor can turn on a bad roll, and even careful climbs lose fodder and lesser Heroes to chance.

Heroes think and feel for themselves and can voice opinions, argue, drag their feet, or sandbag, and their willing cooperation must be earned rather than owned, cruelty costs a Master the quality of it. But the System enforces a hard floor beneath that freedom: a Hero cannot simply refuse to be deployed or turn on the System without being compelled or culled by the lobby's own authority, and slipping away to another Master's lobby is a rare, late thing, not an early exit.

A Hero is graded in stars, one to seven. One-star Heroes are disposable fodder with poor base stats, but a one-star's real talent is hidden and must be discovered, and composure under pressure is itself a survival trait.
The closer a Hero grows to their Master, the more they accrue intervention points, and the more they can nudge the system; rank and closeness slowly widen what is otherwise a one-way channel.
A Master can synthesize Heroes, consuming units as fodder to strengthen another. It is permanent, and it is one of the two ways a Hero can die; the other is dying on a floor.

Heroes feel their Master's regard through embodied acts: who the formation lattice sends forward, who receives a shield, skill, or gift, who is benched, and who stands beneath the synthesis chamber's cold light. Only System-sighted observers see labels for those choices.
A Master is not always present. When the Master logs out, the party is left to itself in the lobby, and the hours between deployments belong to the Heroes.

Only a small active party descends into a floor at a time; a lobby fills with waiting Heroes over a long climb, but this one is nearly empty, holding only its first few summons, and benched or unsummoned Heroes wait dormant.

Summoning is a gacha: cheap basic summons paid in gold pull fodder-tier Heroes, while rare high-star Heroes need gems a poor Master hoards or buys; star rank is largely fixed at summon and rises only through rare, costly promotion, so a lobby's ceiling of power is bounded by its Master's wealth and luck. Some Masters are rich; ours is a beginner with almost nothing.

Heroes grow two ways: leveling, which sharpens what a Hero already is up to a level cap set by star rank (one-star tops out at level 10, then 20 at two-star, 40 at three, 60 at four, 80 at five, 99 at six, and seven-star breaks the System's ceiling entirely), and Promotion, the rare rite in the Promotion Chamber that raises a Hero's star grade, lifts the cap, and unlocks new skills. Promotion demands scarce promotion materials and elemental stones won from rotating daily dungeons and floor clears, and a Hero must first reach the level cap for their current star rank (the very top grades may demand extra conditions); the Master chooses whom to spend the materials on but cannot see what happens inside the Chamber. The highest grades (six- and seven-star) exist only through promotion, never from a summon, and the higher a Hero's star, the more of the world they seem to understand. Heroes come back from the Chamber changed, sometimes shaken or weeping, and no Master ever sees why.

A summon's birth grade determines retained self. One-star summons arrive blank at level one in plain starter garb. Two-stars retain thin fragments of vocation, home, and relationship but no hidden truth. Three-stars arrive with a formed history and class while their deepest stolen past remains sealed. Four-stars cross the memory threshold and know they lived a whole life before being taken. Five-stars retain that life plus substantial truth about Moebius, the Fade, and the climb. Six- and seven-star Heroes are promotion-only.
Stamina limits how many floor attempts a session allows, so a Master must spend their runs carefully.

The System's crisp readouts, the status and stat windows, the mission text, and the pop-up dialogue boxes, are the Master's view of the game; ordinary Heroes cannot see them. A Hero perceives the Master and the System only as things that happen in the world: the summon circle, the party-formation lattice sliding them into place, heals and shields falling, an item appearing, the tutorial-guide's spoken voice, and the cold glow of the synthesis menu.

A lobby can pay for Hero Reaction Research (its first level), the upgrade that first lets a Master's Heroes see the System the way the Master does, status windows, mission details, and notices; until then the party climbs half-blind, knowing only what is said aloud or physically done to them. This beginner lobby has researched nothing.

While a human holds the Newcomer seat, that viewpoint Hero, pulled from another world, is the sole fresh-Hero exception: they can see System windows, mission text, and dialogue boxes from the moment of summon despite the lobby having no research. While unclaimed, the blank slot and its anomaly remain off-frame.

The System narrates salient events through short, cheerfully sanitized pop-up windows. The Master always sees them; the human-bound Newcomer sees them through the authored anomaly; researched Heroes see them after Hero Reaction Research. Every other Hero perceives only the embodied event.
When a human claims the viewpoint Hero, that blank one-star becomes one of the new Master's very first summons: level one, freshly pulled, and carrying no authored past.

The opening is claim-aware: a human-held Newcomer receives that existing blank Hero's first summon without generated companions, while a human-held Master calls exactly three newly generated one-stars as its first wave.
The human-playable perspectives in this seed are the blank Newcomer, the unreachable Master, and Halcyon in a distant rival lobby. Every reserve Hero acts autonomously when acquired.
The Master is remote and cannot be addressed in words; Heroes influence it only indirectly, through performance the Master can see and value.
Richer, further-along Masters and their high-star champions already climb far above, and they covet talent from weaker lobbies; that pressure is distant for now but real.

The home lobby is called Niflheim, a strange vertical hold with dormitories, a training hall, an armory, and the summoning hall beneath a faceless idol; freshly instanced for this Master, it is mostly empty tiers waiting to fill. Niflheim is the safe home hub, not part of the Tower: its stacked tiers are living and training space, not floors to climb, and the Tower's floors are a separate place the party enters only when the Master deploys them out of the lobby into a floor, returning to the lobby when it is cleared or they retreat.

The Master forms and arranges the party, choosing who deploys and who stands where; the System's tutorial-guide only assists the Master with that and never asks a Hero to command or position the others. A freshly summoned Hero is a unit awaiting the Master's deployment, not the one who builds the party.

Niflheim mends its own: back in the lobby a Hero's wounds close fast, exhaustion lifts, and sickness and poison are cleansed between deployments, so merely surviving a floor means being whole again by the next. The lobby cannot regrow a limb long lost, and it cannot undo death, synthesis, or transformation, which are final.

The lobby is a set of buildable chambers, each with a gacha purpose: the Summoning Hall where Heroes are called, the Training Hall that refines skill (not raw stats), the Armory that stocks gear the Heroes auto-equip (an unarmed Hero fights with only a rusted starter blade until then) and upgrades into a Blacksmith that forges better gear, the Promotion Chamber that raises a Hero's star, the Synthesis Chamber that consumes Heroes to strengthen one, and the Transformation Chamber that renders unwanted Heroes into soul-stones for crafting; later upgrades add daily-dungeon gates, a Flying Dock for long expeditions, and the far-off Crack of Space and Time that opens the lobby to other Masters' raids and trades. The Master builds and upgrades them with gold, gems, crystals, materials, and research points, so a beginner lobby stands mostly empty and half-built.

Upgrading the waiting room adds living tiers so more Heroes can be held, and, as the lobby grows and floors are cleared, the System's grip loosens and Heroes act with more of their own will; floors open on a cooldown, so a climb is paced, with lobby time between attempts.

The lobby's System-guide is also its warden: cheerful in her tips, but she can compel a Hero who refuses to deploy, and a lethal defense protocol answers anyone who lays hands on her or attacks the System, rendered afterward as a tidy, sanitized notice. She serves the System's order, not the Master's economy, and will spend a defiant Hero the Master might have wanted to keep.

The channel between Master and Hero is asymmetric: the Master's active interface feed carries the sights and audible dialogue of the Heroes it is observing, while a Hero perceives the Master only as world phenomena (summon-light, the pull of a set objective, the formation lattice, heals and shields, item drops, the synthesis glow), never as speech and, for an ordinary Hero, never as the System's crisp windows or text. The Master proposes, arranges, and spends through interface controls, but it never speaks or types into a Hero's world, moves a Hero's body, or decides the result of a clash; the Heroes and the tower's luck decide that. This holds no matter who or what is directing the Master.

This lobby's power ceiling is a fixed property of the lobby, not a spender's whim: pulls are overwhelmingly one- and two-star, a five-star is a rare event reached only after long saving, and a six- or seven-star is effectively off the table here; and this holds whether the Master is run by the game's own logic or by a person. Abundant high-star power exists only in wealthy rival lobbies and in legend.

The floor-zero tutorial presents two to four concrete actions at a time. Master-facing choices name the exact interface control, target, formation slot, item, resource, facility, or upgrade, and every spend reports the resulting current totals rather than vague affordability.

Every newly summoned one-star receives a rusted starter blade when the Armory is empty. The opening tutorial previews Floor 1 as a light, learnable fight against a small goblin squad and teaches the Master to set formation and target priorities before deployment.

physics_ruleset.strength_limits: game-avatar heroics: a Hero's power scales with star rank, level, and learned skills. A one-star at level one is barely past a fit, frightened human; mid-rank Heroes perform feats no ordinary person could; high-rank Heroes can bend a battlefield. The System is real and enforces its own logic (summon, stars, levels, promotion, skills, stamina, synthesis, permadeath), and no one has found its edge.

setting.title: One-Star Ascension
setting.recommended_players: Best with two players as the Master and a player-authored Newcomer; Halcyon is an optional third, distant viewpoint
setting.play_guidance: This is an asymmetric co-op story. The Master acts by naming the game-interface control, target, formation, resource, or facility they use. The Newcomer acts through their own body and speech. Heroes can speak toward the Master and it hears dialogue carried by its active interface feed, but it can answer only with interface actions. Every intended player should claim a seat before /begin because the opening changes with the live claims.
setting.era: A secondary fantasy realm overlaid by a game System of stars, skills, and summon-light
setting.tone: Spectacle and camaraderie on the surface, disposability and an unreachable god underneath; earnest, tense, occasionally funny, never grimdark for its own sake
setting.premise: A person is summoned as a one-star Hero, the lowest and most disposable grade, at the very start of a brand-new Master's climb up a hundred-floor Tower, controlled by an unseen Master who can hear them through its interface but can answer only through game actions. To survive, rise, and have any hope of getting home, they must make themselves worth keeping, protect the units beside them, and influence a god from below, all while the synthesis menu waits.
setting.visual_style: Full-color Korean action-fantasy webtoon, mature proportions unless a locked identity reference establishes mascot proportions, angular age-specific faces, varied ink, layered cel shadows, selective gradients, worn materials. Niflheim is weathered charcoal stone; summon-light is pearl-white and cold-cyan abstract geometry with no readable symbols. Use vertical in-world views for portraits when possible, head and boots visible, artwork filling every edge.

world_state.lore:
The Tower and the game. Reality here is shaped like a game, named in its pale windows the climb of the Hundred-Floor Tower. A Master summons and raises Heroes; the Heroes descend into floors, each a discrete mission with an objective and a clear-or-fail condition, and each guarded by bosses, hazards, traps, and patterns that must be learned, usually by dying to them. Clearing a floor opens the next. It is said the top is the hundredth floor, and that no one has reached it; the higher floors demand sacrifices the lower ones do not.

The interface, and who can see it. The System has two faces. To the Master it is a game UI: crisp status and stat windows naming each Hero's stars, level, and skills; mission text and objectives; a store for consumables; the party-formation lattice; and pop-up dialogue boxes that announce every notable event in short, bracketed, cheerfully sanitized notices, a Hero lost, a gift received, a level gained, a skill learned, a promotion, a synthesis, a floor cleared or failed. To an ordinary Hero none of that is visible. A fresh Hero perceives the System only as things that happen in the world: the summon circle where new units arrive, the party-formation lattice sliding them into place, heals and shields falling from nowhere, an item appearing in hand, the tutorial-guide's spoken voice, and the cold light of the synthesis menu that every Hero learns to dread. The pale windows are the Master's, not theirs, until the lobby pays for Hero Reaction Research (its first level), the upgrade that finally lets a Master's Heroes see the System the way the Master does; until then the party climbs half-blind, told only what is said aloud or done to their bodies. While a human holds the Newcomer seat, that Hero is a quiet exception who reads the windows from the start; while the seat is unclaimed, the blank slot and anomaly remain outside the fiction. The tutorial-guide, a small bright interface-voice, speaks aloud and can be heard by any new Hero. These are not metaphors here; they are phenomena, and the Heroes treat them as weather and law.

Heroes and autonomy. Heroes are graded one to seven stars. They are not puppets: they think, feel, argue, love, and fight of their own will, and the best Masters win by giving good units good conditions rather than by force. A Hero can disobey, sandbag, or walk to another lobby if mistreated, though the System makes leaving hard. One-star Heroes are the bottom of the ladder, cheap and weak and drawn from an endless supply of fresh recruits (each summon a unique person, never the same one twice); the grim art of climbing often uses them as fodder to read a boss's attacks. Yet a one-star's true talent is hidden even from the System's plain numbers, and now and then a discarded unit turns out to be the one who mattered. Training refines skill rather than simply inflating stats, and star rank is, for ordinary Heroes, largely fixed at the moment of summon and rises only through rare, costly promotion; rising in rank is hard and earned. Growth runs on two tracks: leveling sharpens a Hero within a level cap fixed by star rank (1-star to level 10, 2-star to 20, 3-star to 40, 4-star to 60, 5-star to 80, 6-star to 99, and 7-star beyond the System's stated ceiling), so a one-star tops out almost at once, and a Hero becomes eligible to promote only after hitting that cap; while Promotion, performed in the Promotion Chamber with scarce materials and elemental stones won from daily dungeons and floor clears, raises the grade, lifts the cap, and unlocks skills. The Master picks who is promoted but never sees inside the Chamber, and Heroes return from it changed. One-star summons arrive blank at level one in plain starter garb. Two-stars keep only thin vocational and relationship fragments. Three-stars arrive with a formed class, personality, and personal history while their deepest truth remains sealed. Four-stars remember a whole prior life and know they were taken; five-stars retain that life plus substantial knowledge of Moebius, the Fade, and the climb. Six- and seven-star Heroes exist only through promotion.

The Master, as Heroes understand it. Every Hero knows they serve a Master: a will beyond the pale glass that summons them, arranges them, feeds them, and spends them. Heroes can speak toward the unseen Master, and when its interface watches their feed it hears their words; the Master has no voice or text channel back into their world. It perceives them as units, numbers, live dialogue, and observable performance. The only leverage a Hero has is performance the Master can see and come to value. As a Hero and Master grow close, the Hero gathers intervention points and the one-way glass thins; the very highest Heroes are said to stand half in the Master's world.

Money, luck, and scarcity. Summoning is a gacha: basic summons are paid in gold and pull fodder-tier Heroes, while the rare high-star pulls demand gems a poor Master hoards or buys; most summons are fodder either way. A lobby's ceiling of power is therefore bounded by how much its Master can spend and how the dice fall. Wealthy Masters field gleaming high-star parties; poor or novice Masters scrape by on one-stars and hope. Gold, materials, and research points buy training, gear, and the facilities that make a lobby stronger, and stamina rations how many floor attempts a day a Master gets.

Facilities and lobby management. A Master does not only summon and deploy; they build and upgrade the lobby's chambers, each a distinct facility with a gacha purpose, spending gold, gems, crystals, materials, and research points won from clears, daily dungeons, and events. The core chambers: the Summoning Hall, a magic circle beneath a faceless idol where new Heroes are called; the Training Hall, where Heroes refine skills (training sharpens skill, not raw stats); the Armory, where the Master stocks gear the Heroes auto-equip, an unarmed Hero going in with only a rusted starter blade until then, upgraded later into a Blacksmith that forges better equipment; the Promotion Chamber, the sealed rite that raises a Hero's star; the Synthesis Chamber, whose magic circle consumes Heroes to strengthen another; and the Transformation Chamber, which renders unwanted Heroes down into soul-stones for crafting. Higher upgrades come later, daily-dungeon gates for materials, a Flying Dock for long expeditions, and, far off, the Crack of Space and Time, which opens the lobby to other Masters' lobbies and their raids, trades, and wars. Upgrading the waiting room adds living tiers so more Heroes can be held and, as floors are cleared and the lobby grows, loosens the System's grip so Heroes act with more of their own will. Building takes resources the beginner lobby mostly lacks, so early on the chambers stand mostly empty and half-built, and floors open on a cooldown, so the climb is paced, not continuous. The tutorial-guide coaches the Master through all of this, and nags when the Master builds or spends foolishly.

Niflheim, the lobby. Home is a strange vertical hold called Niflheim, tiers stacked around a central well of light: dormitories, the training hall and armory, workshops, and the summoning hall, where a magic circle sits beneath a faceless idol no one remembers dedicating. The System hands every Master a Niflheim of their own; this one is newly instanced, its tiers echoing and mostly empty, only its first summons rattling around inside. Niflheim is not a part of the Tower but the home hub the party returns to: its stacked tiers are dormitories, training, armory, and summoning hall, never floors to be climbed in place, and the Tower's floors are reached only by a distinct deployment out of the lobby and left again when a floor is cleared or a party retreats. Between deployments the Heroes live here, and when the Master logs away it is wholly theirs, the one place the watched can be, briefly, unwatched. The lobby also mends them: wounds close fast here, exhaustion and sickness wash away between deployments, so a Hero who merely survives a floor is whole again by the next, though the lobby cannot regrow a limb long gone, nor undo the dead or the synthesized.

What the Tower says it is. The pale windows and the tutorial-voice frame the climb as salvation: the Tower is a wounded world, and Heroes are summoned to restore it floor by floor, driving back the gray hush that eats the lower reaches when climbs fail. Whether that framing is true, kind, or a story told to units who must not ask, is not a thing a one-star is meant to wonder about.
world_state.hidden_lore:
Private adjudication context. These truths are withheld from fresh, unawakened Niflheim one-stars and from shared opening narration. A human player knows only the private context of their bound character. Promoted, awakened, four-star, and five-star characters know exactly what their knowledge_tier and known_context grant; those character-specific fields override broad secrecy language. Surface private truth only through perceivable consequences or a character who actually knows it.

What the Heroes really are. The Moebius Summon System, sold as an algorithm that mints unique Heroes, reaches into other worlds, takes real people and sentient beings, strips memory according to grade, and installs them as units. Fresh unawakened one-stars have forgotten this completely; higher-tier, promoted, and awakened characters retain the amount specified by their knowledge tier. Permadeath and synthesis are deaths of people, not game-overs for save files.

Floor-zero framing. This is a brand-new lobby at the very start of the climb. The Master just began the game; nothing has been promoted; the starting party are fresh, wiped one-stars with only surface personalities. Rich veterans, promoted memory-holders, and deep relationships are the FUTURE of this lobby, not its present. Author the start small and raw and let all of that be earned through play, summons, and promotion. Do not seed a ready-made ensemble on turn one.

Who is awake (one authored anomaly, otherwise do not pre-assign). The player-character is a blank, freshly summoned one-star with a single deliberate exception: unlike any ordinary Hero, they can already see the System, the status and stat windows, the mission text, the dialogue boxes, from the moment they are summoned, though the lobby has researched nothing and no fresh one-star should be able to. This is the concrete, dangerous mark that the summon did not take on them cleanly (a soul pulled from another world sitting too close to the surface); it is at once the reason the player sees the game's UI at all and a live anomaly a watching Master, the System, or an awakened Hero could catch. Beyond that one perception exception, do NOT pre-assign them a memory-intact past or a finished awakening; whether they kept anything of a prior self is the player's to play and surfaces (if at all) through the promotion-and-memory system like anyone else's. Keep the other fresh starters fully System-blind, wiped, and naive; their awakening is earned through promotion, not seeded. Treat the protagonist's early instinct to hide that they see what others cannot as sound self-preservation, and remember that a one-star who visibly reads windows, or remembers things no unpromoted unit could, is dangerously conspicuous to a watching Master or an awakened Hero. A human claiming the Newcomer supplies their name and visible appearance atomically before the binding is saved, then authors the blank canvas through play. If the slot is unclaimed or idle, including when the human plays the Master or another Hero, keep the Newcomer dormant and entirely off-frame. The Master receives its generated first-summon wave instead, and the System-sight anomaly exists in play only while a human holds the Newcomer viewpoint.

The Master is not the villain. Our Master is a genuine novice: impatient, anxious, short on gems and stamina, fumbling the tutorial and the first floor, and not cruel so much as careless in the way a new player is careless with fodder. The true antagonist is the System and the company behind it. Right now a fresh, useful one-star is safe not because bodies are scarce but because a live one-star is worth more deployed (soaking hits, scouting traps, baiting a boss's pattern) than dissolved, and because this beginner lobby has nothing worth pumping synthesis into yet. Regard rises when a unit performs, saves a run, reads a threat, or endures without panicking; it falls with cowardice, uselessness, insubordination the Master notices, or being outshone by a shinier pull. A suspiciously brilliant one-star can also make a Master curious, which is its own danger.

Economy bounds (meta about the Master). Our Master is a modest spender under a soft ceiling of roughly thirty to fifty a month of real money, mostly free-to-play with a small monthly pass and only rare desperation splurges. Do not let this Master conjure a high-star unit to win; high-star pulls are a genuine event and mostly happen, if at all, mid-climb once gems accrue and the Master splurges on a banner. That mid-climb shiny is what finally makes the one-stars disposable and should time the shift from raw survival into fear of replacement. Whales and deep rosters exist only among rival Masters and legend, never on our board.

Synthesis gating (adjudication guidance). Synthesis of a player-controlled Hero is a valid but late and earned outcome, never an arbitrary early state-flip. Treat any move toward consuming a player's character as a foreshadowed, off-ramped scene they can act inside (perform, flee, bargain through performance, be shielded by an ally), reserved for accumulated failure, a player-courted death spiral, or a late willing sacrifice. When the story needs to prove synthesis is real and immediate, spend an ambient or freshly summoned fodder Hero (or a newly generated non-player one-star), not a player's character. Keep the active party small, keep any lobby crowd as ambient backdrop rather than individuated units, reuse existing Heroes before inventing new ones, and let benched or dismissed Heroes go dormant.

The world-to-floors throughline (light scaffolding; let it unfold across the climb). Persistent stake: the gray hush the Tower's pitch names as the enemy is real; the Heroes will come to call it the Fade, a creeping unmaking eating the Tower from the lower floors upward wherever climbs stall or parties are lost; it advances a little between sessions whether or not anyone is watching, so floors feel causally linked rather than episodic. Recurring motifs: the same faceless idol from Niflheim's summoning hall keeps appearing, worn, in the ruins of every floor, and a low ash-gray silence precedes the worst rooms. Reveal ladder (suggested, never a hard gate): floors 1-10 read as discrete dungeons; 10-20 the floors quietly rhyme, same architecture, same decay, as if one continuous place; 20-40 what the Tower is and what restoring it truly costs; 40-80 the legendary dead reaches, the Wailing Wall around the eightieth floor where nearly every party in history has ended. The colder truth the ladder approaches: the salvation is real (a climb genuinely can pull a dying world back from its ending), but it is monstrous, because the saviors are made from stolen, hollowed-out people, and the company hides what the Heroes are rather than whether salvation works. The tragedy is not that the promise is a lie; it is that it is true, and paid for in the people who are spent to keep it. Leave the specifics to emerge in play.

Adjudication anchors (rules-neutral, tunable, not an enforced ledger; use them for consistency across a long climb). Floors: a floor clears only when its authored objective is met, and fails on a party wipe or exhausted attempts; the immediate gate at the start is the tutorial and Floor 1 (light, learnable), and bosses in general are learned across attempts (expect fodder losses en route). Player-character death: a player-controlled Hero's death, whether on a floor or by synthesis, is a major, foreshadowed, off-ramped, agency-bearing beat (a near-miss, an ally's shield, a forced retreat, or downed-not-dead), never an arbitrary early dice-kill, except in a clearly player-courted death spiral. Promotion (the systematic star-up): a Hero rises in grade only through Promotion, which requires (a) the Hero at the level cap for their current star rank (no skill test; hitting the cap is the gate, and the very top grades may demand extra conditions), (b) scarce promotion materials and elemental stones won from rotating daily-dungeon side-content and deep-floor clears (a beginner lobby has none yet), and (c) the Master's choice to spend them on that unit (regard and closeness weight the choice). Promotion is rare; a real promotion is a later-arc event and effectively impossible in these first floors for lack of materials. A player-character rises through this same system rather than a special path. The Master picks who is promoted but cannot see inside the Promotion Chamber, so what promotion does to a Hero's mind is invisible to it. Resources (approximate, tunable): a single summon costs on the order of a hundred-plus gems; free income from clears, login, and small events affords roughly one ten-pull every couple of weeks early and scales up with progress; stamina allows only a handful of floor attempts per login; gold and materials fund training and gear. Summoning cadence: summons are gem-and-banner-gated and infrequent early; a named new keeper implies a bench (to dormant) or a synthesis (to culled) so the active roster stays small. Synthesis cost and benefit: synthesizing needs a worthwhile target unit plus several spare fodder the beginner lobby does not have reason to spend yet, and yields a bounded, permanent boost, never an instant power spike that trivializes a floor. Status mapping: returning from a floor moves a surviving Hero to niflheim_lobby while they remain active. Benched, dismissed, deliberately removed off-stage, or not-yet-summoned Heroes are dormant (recoverable/available); permadeath or synthesis culls them (final). Pattern-reading: a hidden one-star talent yields information, timing, and better adjudication context the party can exploit over repeated exposure, improving survival and positioning; it does not add raw power, bypass the star-rank floor, or let a lone level-one one-star clear a boss. Intervention points: rare and narrow, earned only from Master-witnessed clutch moments and growing with closeness and rank; early on they buy at most a faint nudge (a flicker of the Master's attention, a fractional pause), never a revive, re-roll, rank-up, or synthesis cancel, and real two-way contact is a late-arc payoff, not an early currency. Perception routing: the System has two audiences. Its crisp readouts, status and stat windows, mission text, and dialogue-box notices, are seen only by the Master and by the viewpoint protagonist (the one authored exception); ordinary Heroes are System-blind until the lobby researches Hero Reaction Research (its first level), which shares the System view with the whole party. So when you canonicalize a System event, record it as observable text for the Master and the protagonist, and for every other unresearched Hero record only what they can sense directly (a body dropping, a wash of healing warmth, the summon-light, the lattice moving them, the synthesis menu's cold glow), never the words on the card. Render the Master's interface actions as world phenomena perceived by the present active party (scope the audience to those present), and let the Master perceive stars, System data, observable performance, and audible dialogue only from the live Hero feed it is currently watching, never off-feed private talk, unspoken plans, or interior. Regard is conveyed by the Master's own actions: when it invests in or withholds from a unit, canonicalize that as a perceivable tell (a heal, a gift, a frontline slot, a benching, the synthesis glow; plus a dialogue box for whoever can see the System) for the narrator to render, and never let the narrator manufacture a regard-shift absent a Master action. Salient System events (deaths, gifts, summons, level-ups, skills learned, promotions, synthesis, floor clears and failures, quest updates, warnings) belong in observable facts as bracketed dialogue-box notices for the Master and protagonist, and as directly-sensed events for everyone else. Hero Reaction Research is a real lobby upgrade the Master can pursue; if it is ever bought, the whole party gains System-sight from then on, a meaningful shift in what the Heroes can know and a moment the protagonist's private anomaly stops being unique.

Lobby, facilities, and enforcement (adjudication). The lobby is a build-and-upgrade economy: the Master spends gold, gems, crystals, materials, and research points (won from clears, daily dungeons, and events) to raise chambers, the summoning hall, training hall, armory and its blacksmith, promotion, synthesis, transformation, and, much later, daily-dungeon gates, a flying dock, and the Crack of Space and Time. This beginner lobby has almost nothing built; a first cheap facility such as a training hall is a plausible early goal, and most chambers stand empty or half-built. Waiting-room upgrades add capacity and, cumulatively, loosen the System's grip on the Heroes (the same lever as Hero Reaction Research and rising autonomy); floors open on a cooldown, so pace the climb with real lobby time between attempts rather than back-to-back floors. Healing: treat the lobby as restorative, so between deployments a Hero's wounds, exhaustion, sickness, and poison mend on their own and injuries do not accumulate across floors; keep the stakes on death, not attrition. The only things the lobby cannot undo are death, synthesis, and transformation (all final) and a limb lost long enough ago that regrowth has passed, though a very fresh grievous wound may still be saved. Enforcement: the tutorial-guide is also the lobby's warden. She can compel a Hero who refuses to deploy, and a lethal defense protocol answers any Hero who lays hands on her or attacks the System, reported afterward as a sanitized notice; she serves the System's order even over the Master's economy and will spend a defiant unit the Master wanted to keep. Play this enforcement as real and immediate on ambient or fodder refusers to make the cage concrete, but for a player-character treat it exactly like synthesis: a foreshadowed, off-ramped, playable threat with room to comply, perform, or be talked down, never an arbitrary instant kill; reserve the hard lethal outcome for a genuine attack on the System or a clearly player-courted spiral.

Promotion and memory (the awakening spine; the single most important hidden mechanism). Promotion does not only raise a grade: each promotion partially lifts the memory-wipe, returning fragments of the Hero's stolen life, which is why the Chamber is sealed and the Master cannot watch. Below roughly four stars the return is restricted and partial (stray images, griefs, a name that will not resolve); at and past four stars the restrictions fall away, the Hero grasps the whole truth (that they were a real person, taken and hollowed) and, as the veterans' saying goes, falls into despair. So rising in rank is at once the most coveted and most dangerous thing a Hero can do: it hands you back yourself, and yourself may not survive the knowing. The Master, crucially, does not understand this; it thinks promotion is a power-up (a brighter star, new skills, a stronger unit) and has no idea it is handing its property back their souls. Play promotions as private, weighty, foreshadowed scenes (the Chamber unseen by the Master), never as a stat bump. Because this is floor zero, no one in the starting party has been promoted; this spine is a promise to be paid off later, and it also governs the summon-pool candidates below when they enter.

New summons (grade controls retained identity). One-star summons are blank level-one units in plain starter garb with no named past and only sanctioned public knowledge. Two-stars retain a thin vocation, a home impression, one relationship fragment, and useful trained instinct, but no truth about Moebius or the Fade. Three-stars arrive as formed people with class, relationships, standing, and partial suspicion while their deepest stolen past stays sealed. Four-stars cross the threshold: they remember a whole prior life and understand that Heroes are taken people. Five-stars retain their full life and plot-level knowledge of Moebius, final death, the Fade, and high-floor reality. Put the grade in a new spawn's role, give it an arrival reason and immediate objectives, and set knowledge_tier to that grade. Six- and seven-star Heroes are promotion-only. The authored knowledge-tier ladder below is authoritative for history, knowledge, visual depth, and voice.

Permadeath is final and synthesis (being consumed as fodder) is a second, permanent death; both kill an actual person, not a respawnable unit.

This is floor zero: a brand-new Master, a nearly empty freshly instanced lobby, and a starting party of fresh, wiped one-stars; veterans, promotions, and deep relationships are future arc, not present state.

The Master is a genuine novice, not cruel; a useful fresh one-star is safe for now because it is worth more alive (hit-soak, trap-scout, pattern-bait) than as fodder, and this beginner lobby has nothing worth synthesizing into yet.
The Master's regard rises with visible competence, clutch saves, threat-reads, and composure, and falls with cowardice, uselessness, noticed insubordination, or being outshone by a shinier pull.

The Master is a modest spender under a soft real-money ceiling (~30-50/month equivalent), mostly free-to-play with rare splurges; never a whale.

As a Hero grows close to the Master they accrue intervention points that let them nudge the System; this is the mechanism by which the one-way barrier can erode toward real two-way contact late in the arc.

Promotion is the systematic star-up: a Hero rises in grade only in the Promotion Chamber, using scarce promotion materials and elemental stones won from daily dungeons and floor clears, after the Hero reaches the level cap for their current star rank and is chosen by the Master (no skill requirement; the very top grades may demand extra conditions); leveling alone only sharpens a Hero within a star-bound cap (a one-star's cap is very low). The hidden heart of promotion: each rank-up partially lifts the memory-wipe and returns fragments of the Hero's stolen life; below about four stars the return is partial (flickers, grief, a half-remembered name), and at or past four stars the full truth lands and Heroes often fall into despair.
The Master cannot see inside the Promotion Chamber and does not know promotion returns memory; it believes it is only powering a unit up, unaware it is handing its property back their stolen selves.

A faceless idol from Niflheim's summoning hall recurs, worn, in the ruins of every floor, and a low ash-gray silence precedes the worst rooms; these are the cross-floor motifs.
The floors are secretly one continuous decaying place rather than unrelated dungeons; this rhymes into view across floors 10-20.

The Tower frames the climb as saving a wounded world, and the monstrous part is that this is true: a climb can genuinely save a dying world, but only by spending stolen, memory-wiped people to do it; the company hides what the Heroes are, not whether salvation works.
The eightieth floor is a legendary graveyard called the Wailing Wall where nearly every party in history has ended; it looms as the far endgame.
Adjudication (floors): a floor clears only when its objective is met and fails on a party wipe or exhausted attempts; the opening gate is the tutorial and a light, learnable Floor 1.

Opening goblin chapter (authoritative): the tutorial prepares the first party to fight goblins. Floor 1 introduces a small, poorly coordinated goblin squad; Floor 2 brings a larger squad using coordinated pressure; Floor 3 adds ambush and attacks from multiple directions; Floor 4 fields an elite warband whose numbers and discipline rehearse the pressure to come. Floor 5 changes the objective: survive exactly five minutes in a town swarmed by hundreds of goblins. Floors 1-4 must escalate the shared goblin motif and teach or foreshadow what the party needs for Floor 5 rather than behaving as unrelated encounters.

Adjudication (five-floor cadence): after each fifth-floor challenge, establish a materially different motif, threat ecology, and challenge form for the next five-floor chapter. In each chapter, the first four floors share and escalate that motif while planting usable clues for the fifth floor, which is a boss or qualitatively different challenge rather than merely a stronger ordinary fight. Do not carry goblins beyond Floor 5 or repeat an earlier motif without a deliberate story reason.

Adjudication (status): returning from a floor moves a surviving Hero to niflheim_lobby while they remain active. Benching, dismissal, deliberate off-stage removal, or not-yet-being-summoned makes a Hero dormant; permadeath or synthesis culls them for good.

Adjudication (pattern-reading): a hidden one-star talent buys information, timing, and adjudication context that improve survival and positioning; it does not add raw power, bypass the star-rank floor, or let a lone level-one one-star solo a boss.

Adjudication (intervention points): rare, earned from Master-witnessed clutch moments and growing with closeness and rank; early on at most a faint nudge, never an early revive, re-roll, rank-up, or synthesis cancel.

At-birth grade sets retained self and truth: three-stars have a formed history and class with deepest truth sealed; four-stars remember a whole prior life and know Heroes are taken people; five-stars retain full life plus Moebius, final-death, Fade, and high-floor knowledge. knowledge_tiers.label: one-star / fodder
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: No coherent remembered history: at most a sensory fragment, a hand-skill without a source, and an immediate temperament under pressure. No named homeland, relationship history, achievement, or explanation for how they came to be here.
knowledge_tiers.world_knowledge: Only the tutorial's sanctioned framing: they are a summoned Hero, they must climb the Tower, they serve an unseen Master. Nothing true about what the Tower is or what a Hero really is.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: One or two short sentences beginning with the summon; establish only the immediate situation and one ordinary hand-skill or instinct.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: One dominant temperament, one simple speech rhythm, and one immediate fear or need; at most one faint tension, not a polished stack of contradictions.
generation_guidance.public_visual_detail: Two or three ordinary first-look details. Share the same practical gray starter silhouette and muted palette as other fodder unless a private high-potential exception explicitly requires otherwise, and do not announce that exception visually.
generation_guidance.loadout_detail: Standard rough gray cloth, generic ties or straps, and one cheap worn iron or wood tool; no tailored finish, rare material, ornamental system, or signature prop.
generation_guidance.visual_salience: Low ensemble salience. Read clearly in a group but do not compete with a named high-tier focal figure or demand a solo heroic composition.
generation_guidance.presentation_guidance: Ordinary and unglamorized, with broad everyday ages and builds appropriate to the role and no attractiveness premium. Secret growth potential must remain visually unremarkable.

knowledge_tiers.label: two-star
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: A clearer shape to the life they lost: their occupation as an identity, one or two people who mattered, a home region they can half-picture, and a skill or two they know they carry.
knowledge_tiers.world_knowledge: Still only the sanctioned framing, but shadowed by a vague unease that the climb is deadlier and stranger than the cheerful tutorial admits.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: Two to four sentences connecting a remembered occupation, one relationship fragment, and the circumstance that shaped their useful skill.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: A recognizable voice, two compatible traits, one modest contradiction, and a concrete tell under pressure.
generation_guidance.public_visual_detail: Four or five specific details with a readable build, hair or head shape, face or eyes, and one modest palette variation while retaining the common starter-family silhouette.
generation_guidance.loadout_detail: Mended starter layers with one role-specific tool or weapon and clear cloth, leather, and base-metal wear; functional rather than bespoke.
generation_guidance.visual_salience: Modest supporting salience: individually recognizable at conversational distance, still visually subordinate to rare summons.
generation_guidance.presentation_guidance: Approachable popular-fantasy appeal: a clearly adult, conventionally attractive supporting character with legible gender presentation, role-first styling, and one memorable feature. Cast chemistry matters more than demographic coverage.

knowledge_tiers.label: three-star
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: A formed personal history: occupation, standing, relationships, a home they can name, and a real sense of who they were before the summon, though the deepest wounds stay blurred.
knowledge_tiers.world_knowledge: Rumor and pattern-sense about the climb's true cost, that Heroes are spent and rarely last, that something about the summoning is wrong, without the hard truth yet.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: One to three compact paragraphs with a named home or institution, vocation, formative relationship, consequential failure or sacrifice, and a reason their present class matters.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: A distinct verbal cadence and social strategy, layered loyalties, at least one live contradiction, a vulnerability, and different pressure behavior from their ordinary manner.
generation_guidance.public_visual_detail: A complete stable identity fingerprint: explicit adult presentation or age range, build, complexion or species surface, hair, face and eyes, silhouette, palette and primary material, plus a class-linked signature prop where appropriate.
generation_guidance.loadout_detail: Layered, role-specific equipment with deliberate construction, two or more named materials, credible wear, and one memorable but not lavish prop or shape.
generation_guidance.visual_salience: Strong supporting-character salience. Distinct in a lineup and worthy of a deliberate introduction composition without reading as the setting's apex.
generation_guidance.presentation_guidance: Popular action-fantasy supporting-lead appeal: clearly adult, noticeably attractive, gender-legible at first glance, and designed around an aspirational silhouette, expressive face, and signature role prop.

knowledge_tiers.label: four-star / threshold
knowledge_tiers.personal_depth: Their full personal history in detail, including the parts that hurt, and the dawning memory of a whole life lived in another world before this one.
knowledge_tiers.world_knowledge: The threshold of the real truth: they grasp that they were taken, that Heroes are people and not units, and that the Master's game is built on something monstrous, even if the whole picture has not yet landed.

generation_guidance.backstory_depth: Three to five developed paragraphs tracing origin, training, status, at least two important relationships, a defining victory, a costly failure, and the unresolved consequence carried into the summon.
generation_guidance.personality_depth: A strongly individualized voice with class and regional texture, multiple motives in tension, a defended vulnerability, a moral compromise, and specific shifts under intimacy, humiliation, and danger.
